blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 13 (Thermoregulation and Osmoregulation), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The process by which living organisms maintain a stable internal environment despite changes in the external environment is:
blocks.explanation: Homeostasis is the vital process by which organisms maintain a stable internal environment despite external changes (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Homeostasis is a vital process by which living organisms maintain a stable internal environment

blocks.prompt: 2 Which group lists the important processes of homeostasis named in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: The important processes of homeostasis are thermoregulation, osmoregulation and excretion (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Important processes of homeostasis are thermoregulation, osmoregulation, and excretion

blocks.prompt: 3 Homeostasis is maintained through the collaboration of:
blocks.explanation: Homeostasis is maintained through three essential elements: receptors, control centre and effectors (13.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Homeostasis is maintained through the collaboration of three essential elements

blocks.prompt: 4 Receptor cells that detect changes in blood pressure are present in the:
blocks.explanation: Receptor cells in the skin detect temperature changes, and those in blood vessels detect changes in blood pressure (13.1.1).

book_ref.quote: receptors cells in the blood vessels can detect changes in blood pressure

blocks.prompt: 5 Specialized structures that detect changes in the internal or external environment and transmit the information to the control centre are:
blocks.explanation: Receptors (sensors) are organs, tissues, cells or subcellular components that detect changes and transmit the information to the control centre (13.1.1).

book_ref.quote: detect changes in the internal or external environment

blocks.prompt: 6 Which of the following act as control centres in homeostasis?

options.text: Brain, spinal cord and endocrine glands

blocks.explanation: The brain, spinal cord and endocrine glands act as control centres; muscles and glands are effectors (13.1.1).

book_ref.quote: The brain, spinal cord and endocrine glands act as control centres in homeostasis

blocks.prompt: 7 The control centre's messages keep the internal environment within a narrow range of:

options.text: set points, which are optimal for the body's function
the values of the surrounding medium

blocks.explanation: Control centres process information and send messages that keep the internal environment within a narrow range of set points, optimal for body function (13.1.1).

book_ref.quote: These set points are optimal for the body

blocks.prompt: 8 Effectors in homeostasis respond by:

options.text: muscles contracting and glands releasing secretions

blocks.explanation: Muscles and glands are effectors: muscles respond by contracting and glands by releasing their secretion, restoring set points (13.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Muscles respond by contracting while glands release their secretion

blocks.prompt: 9 When body temperature drops below the set point, effectors in the skin and muscles cause:
blocks.explanation: Shivering and vasoconstriction increase heat production and raise the body temperature to the set point (13.1.1).

book_ref.quote: effectors in the skin and muscles cause shivering and vasoconstriction

blocks.prompt: 10 Regulatory processes in which the output of a system is used to control the behaviour of the system itself are called:
blocks.explanation: Feedback mechanisms, the foundations of homeostasis, use the output of a system to control the system itself; there are two types (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: the output or product of a system is used to control the behavior of the system itself

blocks.prompt: 11 The most common form of regulation in the body is:
blocks.explanation: In negative feedback the output reduces the activity of the system; it is the most common form of regulation (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: It is the most common form of regulation

blocks.prompt: 12 Which of these is regulated by negative feedback?
blocks.explanation: Negative feedback regulates body temperature, blood glucose and hormone secretion; childbirth and clotting use positive feedback (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: Common examples of negative feedback include the regulation of body temperature

blocks.prompt: 13 In the negative feedback control of body temperature, once sweating lowers the temperature to the set point:

options.text: the sweat glands secrete more sweat
the thermoreceptors stop sending messages to the control centre

blocks.explanation: The output (lowered temperature) influences the thermoreceptors negatively, so they stop sending messages to the control centre (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: As a result, the thermoreceptors stop sending message to the control centre

blocks.prompt: 14 If body temperature exceeds 37°C, the change is detected by thermoreceptors in the:
blocks.explanation: Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise and signal the thermoregulator (control centre) in the hypothalamus (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: the thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus of brain detect this change

blocks.prompt: 15 A positive feedback system:

options.text: reduces the activity of the system
keeps a variable at its set point
is the most common form of regulation

blocks.explanation: In positive feedback the output increases the activity of the system, enhancing the original stimulus; it is less common than negative feedback (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: In this way, the positive feedback enhances the original stimulus

blocks.prompt: 16 During childbirth, the hormone released by the pituitary gland that stimulates further contractions of the uterus is:
blocks.explanation: Uterine contractions send impulses to the hypothalamus, which signals the pituitary to release oxytocin; oxytocin causes more contractions until the baby is born (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: The control centre sends signals to pituitary gland to release oxytocin hormone

blocks.prompt: 17 Positive feedback often occurs in processes that require:

options.text: rapid and significant changes, e.g. blood clotting

blocks.explanation: Positive feedback occurs in processes needing rapid and significant changes, e.g. blood clotting, labour and childbirth (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: It often happens in the processes that require rapid and significant changes

blocks.prompt: 18 In severe inflammation or infection, unregulated positive feedback can lead to tissue damage due to proteins released by immune cells called:
blocks.explanation: Immune cells release cytokines that further stimulate the immune response; unregulated, this causes excessive inflammation and tissue damage (13.1.2).

book_ref.quote: the immune cells release proteins called cytokines

blocks.prompt: 19 The maintenance of the balance of water and solutes in the body fluids is called:
blocks.explanation: Osmoregulation keeps body fluids from becoming too dilute or too concentrated (13.2).

book_ref.quote: The maintenance of the balance of water and solutes in the body fluids is called osmoregulation

blocks.prompt: 20 Osmoregulation is essential for:

options.text: only the formation of uric acid
proper blood pressure, organ function and regulation of metabolism

blocks.explanation: Osmoregulation is essential for physiological processes including proper blood pressure, proper organ function and regulating metabolism (13.2).

book_ref.quote: including maintaining proper blood pressure

blocks.prompt: 21 The osmotic pressure of a solution is a measure of its tendency to:
blocks.explanation: Osmotic pressure measures a solution's tendency to take in water by osmosis; osmosis goes from hypotonic to hypertonic solution (13.2).

book_ref.quote: The osmotic pressure of a solution is a measure of its tendency to take in water by osmosis

blocks.prompt: 22 Osmoconformers remain, with respect to their environment:
blocks.explanation: Osmoconformers cannot maintain their water and solute concentrations, which change with the medium, so they remain isotonic to it (13.2.1).

book_ref.quote: they remain isotonic to their environment

blocks.prompt: 23 Which of the following are osmoconformers?
blocks.explanation: Osmoconformers include all marine invertebrates, some freshwater invertebrates and some marine vertebrates like hag fishes, sharks and rays (13.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Examples of osmoconformers include all marine invertebrates

blocks.prompt: 24 Osmoconformers are usually found in environments with:

options.text: relatively stable solute concentrations, such as marine water

blocks.explanation: Osmoconformers usually live where solute concentrations are relatively stable, such as marine water (13.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Such animals are usually found in environments with relatively stable solute concentrations

blocks.prompt: 25 Animals that maintain constant internal concentrations of water and solutes despite a changing environment are:
blocks.explanation: Osmoregulators regulate water and solute concentrations; most vertebrates in water and on land are osmoregulators (13.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Most vertebrates in aquatic and terrestrial environments are osmoregulators

blocks.prompt: 26 Which of the following is a mechanism used by osmoregulators?
blocks.explanation: Osmoregulators use mechanisms such as active transport of salts, accumulation of salts and water conservation (13.2.1).

book_ref.quote: active transport of salts, accumulation of salts, and water conservation

blocks.prompt: 27 Freshwater animals are generally:
blocks.explanation: Freshwater animals have a higher solute concentration in body fluids than the surrounding water, i.e. they are hypertonic (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Generally, the freshwater animals are hypertonic to their environment

blocks.prompt: 28 The problem of salts faced by freshwater animals is that:

options.text: salts diffuse into the body from water
they drink too much salt water
salts and ions like Na⁺ and Cl⁻ diffuse out of the body
uric acid crystals form in gills

blocks.explanation: Essential salts and ions like Na⁺ and Cl⁻ diffuse out into the water; they compensate by actively transporting salts back in (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Essential salts and ions (like Na⁺ and Cl⁻) diffuse out of the body

blocks.prompt: 29 To eliminate the excess water that enters their bodies, freshwater animals:

options.text: produce small amounts of concentrated urine
produce large volumes of diluted urine

blocks.explanation: Freshwater animals produce large volumes of diluted urine and rarely drink water (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: For this purpose, they produce large volumes of diluted urine

blocks.prompt: 30 In hypotonic marine animals, excess salts are actively pumped out of the blood into the environment by:
blocks.explanation: Specialized chloride cells in the gills use ATP to actively pump salts out of the blood back into the environment (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: specialized chloride cells in the gills use energy (ATP)

blocks.prompt: 31 Rectal glands of some marine fishes:

options.text: remove salts from blood into the digestive tract, eliminated with faeces

blocks.explanation: Rectal glands remove salts from blood into the digestive tract, and the salts are eliminated with faeces (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Some marine fishes also have special salt excreting glands in rectum called rectal glands

blocks.prompt: 32 Hypotonic marine animals conserve water by producing:

options.text: very small amounts of highly concentrated urine

blocks.explanation: They produce very small amounts of highly concentrated urine; excess salts also leave through the kidneys (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: They also conserve water by producing very small amounts of highly concentrated urine

blocks.prompt: 33 The impermeable outer layer of reptiles that prevents evaporative water loss is made of:
blocks.explanation: Insects have a waxy chitin exoskeleton, reptiles waterproof keratin scales, and mammals and birds dead keratinized skin cells with oil glands (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Reptiles have waterproof scales made of keratin

blocks.prompt: 34 The Kangaroo Rat can survive entirely on:

options.text: metabolic water produced by cellular respiration

blocks.explanation: The Kangaroo Rat survives entirely on metabolic water, a by-product of cellular respiration (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: survive entirely on metabolic water

blocks.prompt: 35 A behavioural adaptation of many desert animals to avoid evaporation is that they:

options.text: bask in the sun all day
stay underground by day and emerge at night

blocks.explanation: They stay underground during the heat of the day and emerge at night when the air is cooler and more humid (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Many desert animals stay underground during the heat of the day to avoid evaporation

blocks.prompt: 36 Tardigrades (water bears) losing almost all their body water and entering a dormant state is called:
blocks.explanation: In anhydrobiosis, certain invertebrates like tardigrades become dormant after losing almost all body water and revive years later when water returns (13.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Certain invertebrates, like tardigrades (water bears), enter a dormant state

blocks.text: 13.2.3 Nature of Excretory Products in relation to Habitat

blocks.prompt: 37 In many animals, osmoregulation is coupled with the removal of:
blocks.explanation: Osmoregulation is coupled with removal of metabolic wastes, mainly nitrogenous wastes (ammonia, urea, uric acid), excreted as water solutes (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: In many animals, osmoregulation is coupled with the removal of metabolic wastes from the body

blocks.prompt: 38 The volume of water needed to dissolve one gram of ammonia to a nontoxic level is:
blocks.explanation: One gram of ammonia requires 500 mL of water; urea needs 50 mL and uric acid just 1 mL (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: One gram of ammonia requires 500 mL of water to dissolve it to nontoxic level

blocks.prompt: 39 Sponges and coelenterates, which excrete ammonia as their major nitrogenous waste, are called:
blocks.explanation: Animals excreting ammonia as their major nitrogenous waste are ammonotelic, e.g. most fishes, protozoans, sponges, coelenterates (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Animals which excrete ammonia as their major nitrogenous wastes are called ammonotelic

blocks.prompt: 40 Ammonia is produced when the amino group (-NH₂) removed from amino acids and nucleic acids combines with:
blocks.explanation: The amino group (-NH₂) removed from amino acids and nucleic acids combines with H⁺ to form ammonia (NH₃) in the liver (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: It is produced when amino group (-NH₂) is removed from amino acids and nucleic acids

blocks.prompt: 41 Ammonia is excreted rapidly because it is:
blocks.explanation: Ammonia is highly toxic, so it is excreted rapidly with plenty of water, which only freshwater animals can afford (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Ammonia is highly toxic and so it is excreted rapidly

blocks.prompt: 42 One gram of urea requires how much water to dilute it to a nontoxic level?
blocks.explanation: Urea is less toxic than ammonia; one gram of urea requires 50 mL of water (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: One gram of urea requires 50 mL water to dilute it to the nontoxic level

blocks.prompt: 43 Terrestrial animals that convert ammonia to urea in the liver and excrete it through the kidneys are called:
blocks.explanation: Animals excreting urea as their major nitrogenous waste are ureotelic (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The animals which excrete urea as their major nitrogenous waste product are called ureotelic

blocks.prompt: 44 In humans, uric acid is a by-product of the breakdown of:
blocks.explanation: Uric acid is a by-product of breakdown of purines (found in meat and some vegetables) and is produced in the liver (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Uric acid is a by-product of the breakdown of purines

blocks.prompt: 45 Excess uric acid in the blood forms crystals in joints and tissues, causing the painful condition:
blocks.explanation: When uric acid is in excess in blood, crystals form in joints and tissues, causing gout (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: causing painful conditions such as gout

blocks.prompt: 46 Birds and most reptiles excrete uric acid. One gram of uric acid requires for its excretion only:
blocks.explanation: Uric acid is less soluble, makes precipitates and needs just 1 mL of water per gram (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: One gram of uric acid requires just 1 mL of water for its excretion

blocks.prompt: 47 The conversion of ammonia into uric acid by insects, birds and desert animals:
blocks.explanation: These animals cannot afford to excrete even urea, so they convert ammonia to uric acid using a lot of energy (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: They convert ammonia to uric acid by using lot of energy

blocks.prompt: 48 Which group of animals is uricotelic?
blocks.explanation: Insects, desert animals, birds and most reptiles excrete uric acid and are called uricotelics (13.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The animals which excrete uric acid are called uricotelics

blocks.prompt: 49 Thermoregulation is the homeostatic process by which organisms maintain their internal body temperature:

options.text: always equal to the external temperature
within a tolerable range, regardless of the external temperature

blocks.explanation: Thermoregulation keeps internal body temperature within a tolerable range regardless of the external temperature (13.3).

book_ref.quote: maintain their internal body temperature within a tolerable range

blocks.prompt: 50 If the temperature rises well above the optimal temperature, enzymes:

options.text: begin to denature and lose their function permanently

blocks.explanation: Well above the optimum, enzymes denature and lose function permanently; below it, enzyme-substrate collisions and metabolic rates drop (13.3).

book_ref.quote: If temperatures rises well above the optimal, enzymes begin to denature

blocks.prompt: 51 Low temperatures affect cell membranes by making them:
blocks.explanation: Low temperatures make membranes rigid and brittle; at high temperatures membranes can lose their selective permeability (13.3).

book_ref.quote: Low temperatures can make membranes rigid and brittle

blocks.text: 13.3.1 Types of Animals on the basis of Heat Source

blocks.prompt: 52 Animals that gain most of their body heat from external sources are:
blocks.explanation: Ectotherms gain most of their body heat from external sources; their temperature fluctuates with the surroundings (13.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Ectotherms are animals that gain most of their body heat from external sources

blocks.prompt: 53 A lizard that is too cold sits on a warm rock. It gains heat by:
blocks.explanation: Ectotherms use behavioural thermoregulation: basking in the sun is radiation, sitting on a warm rock is conduction (13.3.1).

book_ref.quote: If they are too cold, they bask in the sun (radiation) or sit on a warm rock (conduction)

blocks.prompt: 54 Ectotherms rely on heat from the environment because:

options.text: their metabolic rate is very low and cannot produce enough heat
they have thick insulation of fat

blocks.explanation: In ectotherms the metabolic rate is very low; they cannot produce enough heat to raise and maintain body temperature (13.3.1).

book_ref.quote: In ectotherms, the metabolism rate is very low

blocks.prompt: 55 In very cold climates, ectotherms survive the coldest months by:
blocks.explanation: In very cold climates ectotherms become dormant during the coldest months (13.3.1).

book_ref.quote: In very cold climates, they become dormant during the coldest months

blocks.prompt: 56 When it gets cold, endotherms may produce heat by shivering or by burning:
blocks.explanation: Endotherms may shiver (muscle contractions) or burn brown adipose tissue for heat when it gets cold (13.3.1).

book_ref.quote: burn brown adipose tissue for heat

blocks.prompt: 57 Endotherms retain heat with insulation such as:
blocks.explanation: Most endotherms have insulation to retain heat, such as hair, feathers or fat (13.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Most endotherms have insulation to retain heat such as hair, feathers, or fat

blocks.text: 13.3.2 Types of Animals on the basis ability of Thermoregulation

blocks.prompt: 58 Animals unable to maintain their body temperature within narrow limits are called:
blocks.explanation: Poikilotherms cannot keep body temperature within narrow limits; it usually matches the environment (13.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Poikilotherms are the animals that are unable to maintain their body temperature within narrow limits

blocks.prompt: 59 An advantage of poikilotherms over homeotherms is that they:
blocks.explanation: Poikilotherms need not consume massive food to 'fuel' a constant temperature, so they survive in nutrient-poor environments where a homeotherm would starve (13.3.2).

book_ref.quote: It allows them to survive in nutrient-poor environments where a homeotherm would starve

blocks.prompt: 60 Homeotherms trigger cooling or heating responses using a 'thermostat', which is the:
blocks.explanation: Homeotherms (mammals, birds) keep constant body temperature using 'thermostats', the hypothalamus in the brain (13.3.2).

book_ref.quote: They use "thermostats" (hypothalamus in the brain) to trigger cooling or heating responses

blocks.prompt: 61 On the basis of heat source and thermoregulation, humans are:
blocks.explanation: Humans are endothermic homeotherms and regulate body temperature through negative feedback (13.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Humans are endothermic homeotherms

blocks.prompt: 62 During hypothermia, vasoconstriction helps because it:

options.text: reduces blood flow to the skin, so less heat is lost
increases blood flow to the skin

blocks.explanation: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin, so less heat is lost from the blood (13.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin

blocks.prompt: 63 When tiny muscles at the base of hair follicles contract (goosebumps), body heat is conserved because:

options.text: air trapped in the erected hair acts as an insulator

blocks.explanation: Contraction of the tiny muscles erects hair; air trapped in it acts as an insulator for heat (13.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Air is trapped in the erected hair and act as insulator for the heat

blocks.prompt: 64 Shivering is:

options.text: spasmodic contraction of skeletal muscles that produces heat

blocks.explanation: Shivering, the spasmodic contraction of skeletal muscles, produces heat that helps raise body temperature (13.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Shivering (spasmodic contraction of skeletal muscles) produces heat

blocks.prompt: 65 During hyperthermia, the thyroid gland may decrease the secretion of thyroxine, which:

options.text: lowers the basal metabolic rate and internal heat production

blocks.explanation: Less thyroxine lowers the basal metabolic rate, so internal heat production is reduced (13.3.3).

book_ref.quote: The thyroid gland may decrease the secretion of thyroxine

blocks.prompt: 66 Sweating cools the body because:

options.text: sweat blocks blood flow to skin
evaporation of sweat carries heat away from the body

blocks.explanation: Evaporation of sweat carries heat from the body and produces a cooling effect (13.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Evaporation of sweat carries heat from the body and produces cooling effect

blocks.prompt: 67 In vasodilation during overheating, more blood flows through the capillaries beneath the epidermis because:

options.text: the arterioles supplying the skin capillaries widen
the heart stops pumping to muscles

blocks.explanation: Capillaries have no muscle and cannot widen themselves; the arterioles supplying them widen, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost (13.3.3, book correction).

book_ref.quote: In vasodilation the arterioles (small arteries) that supply the skin capillaries widen

blocks.prompt: 68 We 'feel' warmth or coldness and take actions like turning on a fan because thermoreceptors also stimulate:

options.text: the higher centres of the brain

blocks.explanation: Thermoreceptors also stimulate higher brain centres, so we feel warmth or coldness and take actions like bathing or using fans or heaters (13.3.3).

book_ref.quote: The thermoreceptors also stimulate the higher centres of brain
